confidence_scale.medium: The benchmark is the same commodity, traded internationally, and a plausible reference for imported supplies of this product. It still differs from the local price in grade, place, stage of the supply chain and currency.
confidence_scale.low: The benchmark is a related but different product or grade, or the local product is mostly produced and traded regionally. A similar movement would be weak evidence and a different movement would not argue against anything.
confidence_scale.none: No credible international benchmark exists for this product among the integrated series.

note: No mapping is rated 'high': a world export quotation and a retail or wholesale price in a local market always differ in transport, tariffs, margins, quality and currency. Mappings are a research convenience, not a statement that the local price follows the benchmark.

limitations: Imported rice in much of West and Central Africa is Thai, Indian, Pakistani or Vietnamese rice, often parboiled or in broken grades; the benchmarks are white-rice export quotations f.o.b. Bangkok or Hanoi, so freight, insurance, port charges, import duties, traders' margins and the grade differences are not captured.
India, the largest exporter, is not a Pink Sheet benchmark and its export policy has moved world rice trade.
The series does not say whether the rice is imported or locally produced; a local product need not follow export quotations at all.
The benchmarks are white-rice export quotations, not retail or wholesale prices.
Locally produced rice is priced in domestic markets; no international benchmark is mapped.
US wheat export prices are one of several international reference prices (Black Sea, EU, Canadian and Australian wheat also trade); the integrated series cover US classes only.
Local wheat is mostly imported grain that is then milled; freight, duties and subsidies are not captured.
Flour and bread include milling, packaging, transport and retail margins and often local policy (flour subsidies, price controls); a wheat grain quotation is a small part of the price.
The benchmark is US yellow maize f.o.b. Gulf; much African maize is white maize, produced and traded regionally, with prices set by local harvests.
A grade, colour and market-structure mismatch means similar movements are weak evidence of transmission.
A milled product: milling margins and local supply dominate; the benchmark is yellow grain.
Sorghum in the Sahel and East Africa is mainly locally produced and consumed; the benchmark is US yellow milo for export.
World raw sugar differs from refined sugar sold locally; many countries protect domestic sugar with tariffs and quotas.
Locally produced sugar is priced domestically; no benchmark is mapped.
Palm oil is widely traded; local palm oil in producing regions is often artisanal and priced locally.
The benchmark is Malaysian export price, not the product sold at retail.
The oil's source (palm, soybean, sunflower, groundnut, blends) is not stated, so which benchmark applies is unknown; the three listed move together only partly.
The benchmark is US runner groundnuts for the European market; groundnuts in Africa are mainly locally produced and consumed.
Local fresh chicken is mostly domestic; the benchmark is Brazilian frozen chicken.
Beef in most WFP countries is local cattle; the benchmark is imported lean beef in the US.
Pump prices include refining, taxes, subsidies and transport and are often administratively set; crude oil is only one component.

no_benchmark_note: Millet, cassava, yams, plantains, pulses, vegetables, fruits, eggs, salt, fresh fish and most other items have no international benchmark among the integrated series; the engine states that no benchmark is mapped and shows nothing in its place.
